{{short description|American mathematician}}
[[File:Eva_Kallin_1974_(headshot).jpg|thumb|Portrait of Eva Kallin Pohlmann]]
'''Eva Marianne Kallin Pohlmann''' is a professor emerita of [[mathematics]] at [[Brown University]]. Her research concerns [[Banach function algebra|function algebra]]s, [[Holomorphically convex hull|polynomial convexity]], and [[Tarski's axioms]] for [[Euclidean geometry]].

Kallin attended the [[University of California, Berkeley]] as an undergraduate, and graduated with an A.B. in mathematics in 1953 and an M.S. in 1956.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=owE5AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA246 Commencement program from Berkeley in 1950] showing Kallin as the freshman recipient of a scholarship; [https://books.google.com/books?id=1AA5AQAAMAAJ&pg=PA121 Commencement program from 1956] showing her with an A.B. in 1953 and an M.S. in 1956.</ref> In 1956–1957, working as a student of [[Alfred Tarski]], Kallin helped simplify [[Tarski's axioms]] for the [[first-order theory]] of [[Euclidean geometry]], by showing that several of the axioms originally presented by Tarski did not need to be stated as axioms, but could instead be proved as theorems from the other axioms.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Tarski | first = Alfred
 | editor1-last = Henkin | editor1-first = L.
 | editor2-last = Suppes | editor2-first = P.
 | editor3-last = Tarski | editor3-first = A.
 | contribution = What is elementary geometry?
 | mr = 0106185
 | pages = 16–29
 | publisher = North-Holland Publishing Co., Amsterdam
 | series = Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics
 | title = The axiomatic method. With special reference to geometry and physics. Proceedings of an International Symposium held at the Univ. of Calif., Berkeley, Dec. 26, 1957-Jan. 4, 1958
 | year = 1959}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Szczerba | first = L. W.
 | doi = 10.2307/2273904
 | issue = 4
 | journal = The Journal of Symbolic Logic
 | mr = 865918
 | pages = 907–912
 | title = Tarski and geometry
 | volume = 51
 | year = 1986| jstor = 2273904
 }}.</ref>

Kallin earned her Ph.D. in 1963 from Berkeley under the supervision of [[John L. Kelley]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=31976}}</ref> Her thesis, only 14 pages long, concerned function algebras, and a summary of its results was published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America|Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]''.<ref>{{MR|2614057}}; {{MR|0152907}}</ref> One of its results, that not every [[topological algebra]] is localizable, has become a "well-known counterexample".<ref>{{citation
 | last = Mallios | first = Anastasios
 | contribution = On localizing topological algebras
 | doi = 10.1090/conm/341/06167
 | mr = 2040018
 | pages = 79–95
 | publisher = Amer. Math. Soc., Providence, RI
 | series = Contemp. Math.
 | title = Topological algebras and their applications
 | volume = 341
 | year = 2004| arxiv = gr-qc/0211032
 | isbn = 978-0-8218-3556-2
 | s2cid = 14378342
 }}. See in particular [https://books.google.com/books?id=lpEbCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA89 p.&nbsp;89].</ref>

In the study of [[complex vector space]]s, a set ''S'' is said to be polynomially convex if, for every point ''x'' outside of ''S'', there exists a polynomial whose complex [[absolute value]] at ''x'' is greater than at any point of ''S''. This condition generalizes the ordinary notion of a [[convex set]], which can be separated from any point outside the set by a linear function. However, polynomially convex sets do not behave as nicely as convex sets. Kallin studied conditions under which unions of convex balls are polynomially convex, and found an example of three disjoint cubical cylinders whose union is not polynomially convex.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Kallin | first = Eva
 | contribution = Polynomial convexity: The three spheres problem
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-48016-4_26
 | mr = 0179383
 | pages = 301–304
 | publisher = Springer, Berlin
 | title = Proc. Conf. Complex Analysis (Minneapolis, 1964)
 | year = 1965| isbn = 978-3-642-48018-8
 }}.</ref> As part of her work on polynomial convexity, she proved a result now known as Kallin's lemma, giving conditions under which the union of two polynomially convex sets remains itself polynomially convex.<ref>{{citation
 | last = De Paepe | first = P. J.
 | doi = 10.1112/blms/33.1.1
 | issue = 1
 | journal = The Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society
 | mr = 1798569
 | pages = 1–10
 | title = Eva Kallin's lemma on polynomial convexity
 | volume = 33
 | year = 2001}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Stout | first = Edgar Lee
 | isbn = 978-0-8176-4537-3
 | mr = 2305474
 | page = 62
 | quote = A union of polynomially convex sets is generally not polynomially convex. There is, however, an important result that affirms the polynomial convexity of a union of two polynomially convex sets under certain hypotheses. It goes back to the work of E. Kallin and is often referred to as Kallin's lemma.
 | publisher = Birkhäuser Boston, Inc., Boston, MA
 | series = Progress in Mathematics
 | title = Polynomial convexity
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=nzKOkwtMSqQC&pg=PA62
 | volume = 261
 | year = 2007}}.</ref>
